items.title: Randy Sandke interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 10, 1997
items.q: hired, got Mike Brecker and Jim McNealy and John Goldsby, Kenny Washington and did all originals in a modern context. That was my first record.

ctx.x: That first time after, picking up the trumpet after ten years, did your chops remember what it felt like? © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

Well yeah kind of, although I was conscious that I wanted to play differently than I had before because if I was going to do this I didn’t want to have the same problem. My fingers, when Mike was teaching me in the beginning said, “I’m used to teaching beginners who don’t know the fingerings, and here, it’s like —.” So I tried to play. I wasn’t trying to play high, loud, anything. But I would just play tunes, middle register things, and I really from the start felt that connection again.
Was your experience with the guitar and the piano, did that help your trumpet improvising?

items.title: Randy Sandke interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 10, 1997
items.q: I went to college with Michael Brecker

ctx.x: It sounds hipper than I thought it was going to be. Nice.

Right. I think the one that really threw people for a loop was the record after this, which had Ray Anderson and Michael Brecker. And the first tune on it was “Lullaby of Broadway.” And I know that some, I think it was Jazzbo Collins, you know he got the record, oh Randy Sandke, well this will be a nice kind of like, you know, easy listening jazz, and put it on, and it’s supposed to be this Kafkaesque picture of, you know, New York at rush hour kind of thing. And so he was a little bit thrown for a loop. So that…
Would you bring in Michael Brecker and that crew and do that at the Aspen festival?
